question: Which statement best describes getDerivedStateFromError?
options: A static lifecycle method that React calls when a descendant throws during rendering. It receives the error and must return a plain state object (e.g. { hasError: true }) that triggers the boundary to re-render with its fallback. Because it runs during the render phase it must be pure — no side effects, no logging, no network calls go here.

Whatever the boundary renders when it is in the error state. A good fallback is more than a bare 'Something went wrong' message — it should be localized to the failed region, match your design system, and ideally offer a recovery action like a retry button. Never render the raw error message or stack trace to end users, since it can leak internal details.

Where you put boundaries determines how tightly failures are contained, because the nearest boundary above a throwing component catches the error. A single global boundary replaces the whole app on any crash, while per-widget and per-route boundaries isolate failures to a small region. The common pattern layers them: per-widget for independently-failing cards, per-route so a page crash stays on that page, and a global catch-all as a last resort.

An instance lifecycle method invoked after a descendant throws, receiving the error and an info object containing the component stack. This is where side effects belong: logging to the console, reporting to a service like Sentry, or incrementing metrics. It does not affect what the boundary renders — that is the job of getDerivedStateFromError.

options: Error Boundaries only catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors. They do NOT catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (setTimeout, promises, async/await), server-side rendering, or errors thrown in the boundary component itself. Those occur outside React's synchronous render phase, so you must handle them yourself with try/catch and surface them via state.

Those occur outside React's synchronous render phase, so you must handle them yourself with try/catch and surface them via state.

Once a boundary is in its error state it stays there until you reset it, since the children won't re-render on their own. The simplest reset is changing the boundary's key prop, which remounts it and gives the children a fresh chance to render. The react-error-boundary library formalizes this with a resetKeys prop and a resetErrorBoundary callback passed to the fallback.
